name: Capstone Project
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Capstone: From a Real Problem to a Defensible Recommendation
lesson.summary: The course's closing chapter runs one realistic problem through the entire pipeline built across this arc, decision flowchart, cost simulation, hybrid architecture, ATAM-based architecture report, recommendation, and executive presentation, while making explicit the five throughlines the whole course was built around.
lesson.body:
This chapter introduces no new blockchain concept. That is deliberate, and it is the point. A capstone at the end of two hundred concepts is not another topic, it's the proof that everything before it was actually usable together, on a single problem, in the order a real organization would need it. If you can run one scenario cleanly through decision flowchart, cost simulation, hybrid architecture, architecture report, recommendation, and presentation, you have demonstrated the actual skill this course was built to teach, which was never memorizing how a Merkle tree works, it was learning to evaluate a trust technology honestly when the pressure in the room is pushing you not to.

Five throughlines have run underneath every chapter of this course, and the capstone is where you should be able to point at each one and name exactly where it did work in your own analysis. Decentralization tradeoffs: every gain in censorship resistance or tamper evidence costs something in performance, cost, or coordination overhead, and there is no configuration that gets all the benefits for free. Governance models: a blockchain does not remove the need for humans to agree on rules, it just makes the rules that get encoded harder to quietly violate, while everything not encoded, dispute resolution, membership changes, liability, still runs through ordinary contracts and institutions. Real versus hyped use cases: the decision flowchart exists specifically to separate a genuine multi-writer, low-trust coordination problem from a use case that sounds impressive in a pitch deck but is actually solved more cheaply by a database and a signature. Cognitive biases in tech evaluation: novelty bias, sunk cost, bandwagon pressure, and authority bias show up at every stage, from the initial flowchart through the executive presentation, and the discipline of sequential gates, traceable evidence, and named alternatives exists specifically to blunt them. And architecture tradeoff analysis: ATAM's habit of turning vague quality goals into concrete scenarios and then finding where those scenarios pull against each other is what separates an architecture report from a sales pitch for whichever option you already preferred.

The capstone assignment itself follows the same shape as the worked example running through this arc. Pick a real problem, either from your own organization or from a scenario provided in the course, and take it through every stage in order, producing an actual document set: a decision flowchart walkthrough with an honest answer at every gate, a cost simulation, a hybrid architecture decision where relevant, an ATAM-based architecture report, a recommendation memo, and a short executive presentation. Skipping a stage, or writing one stage's conclusion before honestly completing the stage before it, defeats the purpose even if the final document looks polished.

Two prerequisites from earlier in the course do heavy lifting here and deserve a direct callback. Cost simulation is not just tallying software licensing against a competitor's quote, it means building a total cost of ownership comparison that includes the true cost of the status quo, in Meridian's case the cost and duration of past recall investigations, against the full cost of the proposed system, including the parts organizations habitually forget: governance meetings, key management, and the staff time needed to operate validator nodes. When Meridian ran this comparison, the finding wasn't just that the pilot was affordable, it was that recording every single temperature reading directly on the permissioned ledger would make the system expensive to run at full scale in a way the pilot's small footprint had hidden.

That finding is what pushed Meridian toward a hybrid architecture: rather than writing every raw reading to the ledger, each party keeps raw readings in their own existing systems, and the network instead commits a cryptographic hash of each batch of readings to the permissioned ledger at fixed intervals. Anyone can later prove a specific reading was part of an unaltered batch by checking it against the committed hash, which delivers the tamper-evidence gate four of the decision flowchart demanded, without paying to store or replicate every raw data point across every validator. This is the general shape hybrid architectures take across most legitimate blockchain use cases: put the minimum on-chain that is actually needed for the tamper-evidence or coordination property you're buying, and keep the bulk of the data where it's cheaper to store and query.

That hybrid decision is not free, and a capstone submission should say so rather than presenting it as a costless improvement. The batch interval becomes a new scenario in the utility tree, since a longer interval between hash commits lowers cost further but also lengthens the window during which a bad actor could, in principle, alter unconfirmed readings before they're locked in, a genuine tradeoff point that the architecture report has to state and justify with the same honesty as the confirmation-threshold tradeoff from the earlier chapter, not gloss over because the hybrid design otherwise looks like an unambiguous win.

From there, the rest of the pipeline runs exactly as taught: the architecture report documents the hybrid design and its tradeoffs, the recommendation memo states the pilot ask up front and traces every claim back to the cost simulation and the flowchart, and the executive presentation compresses all of it into five slides built to survive the bandwagon and authority-bias questions a management audience predictably asks.

One last point belongs at the very end of this course, and it is the one most worth remembering after the specific gates and slide structures are forgotten. This book is called a skeptic's guide, and a correct no is exactly as strong a capstone outcome as a correct yes. If your honest run through the decision flowchart lands on stop at gate three because the parties in your scenario already share a trusted intermediary, that is not a failed capstone, it's the flowchart doing precisely what it was built to do. The skill this entire course was built to teach was never advocacy for a technology. It was the discipline to look at a real coordination problem, follow the evidence through gates that don't bend to pressure, and be equally willing to write the recommendation that says build it or the one that says don't, and defend either with the same rigor.
